coverage.explain: Reads, writes, syncs and opens of files: data files, redo and undo logs, binary logs, temporary files.
coverage.label: File I/O

coverage.explain: Row operations through the storage engine interface (fetch, insert, update, delete). Each wait covers the whole engine call, so file I/O and internal lock waits inside it are counted here and again under their own events. InnoDB row lock waits have no event of their own and are inside this time too (Locks shows them).
coverage.label: Table I/O

coverage.explain: Table lock requests: THR_LOCK table locks (MyISAM, MEMORY, LOCK TABLES) and each storage engine external lock call. For InnoDB this is the per-statement table lock call, which includes waits for LOCK TABLES; row lock waits are not here.
coverage.label: Table locks

coverage.explain: Waits for metadata locks: DDL waiting for open transactions, or statements waiting behind DDL, LOCK TABLES or FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK.
coverage.label: Metadata locks

enable.runtime: UPDATE performance_schema.setup_instruments SET ENABLED = 'YES', TIMED = 'YES' WHERE NAME LIKE 'wait/synch/mutex/%';

coverage.explain: Short-term internal locks that protect shared memory structures.
coverage.label: Mutexes

enable.runtime: UPDATE performance_schema.setup_instruments SET ENABLED = 'YES', TIMED = 'YES' WHERE NAME LIKE 'wait/synch/rwlock/%';
UPDATE performance_schema.setup_instruments SET ENABLED = 'YES', TIMED = 'YES' WHERE NAME LIKE 'wait/synch/sxlock/%';

coverage.explain: InnoDB's shared/exclusive internal locks, such as an index tree's lock.
coverage.label: Shared/exclusive locks

enable.runtime: UPDATE performance_schema.setup_instruments SET ENABLED = 'YES', TIMED = 'YES' WHERE NAME LIKE 'wait/synch/cond/%';

coverage.explain: Threads waiting to be signalled by another thread (for example a group commit).
coverage.label: Condition waits

enable.runtime: UPDATE performance_schema.setup_instruments SET ENABLED = 'YES', TIMED = 'YES' WHERE NAME LIKE 'wait/io/socket/%';

coverage.explain: Network reads and writes on client and replication connections.
coverage.label: Socket I/O

enable_caveat: The UPDATE takes effect at once, for existing and new instances, and lasts until the server restarts; the my.cnf line (under [mysqld]) keeps it after a restart. Waits already in progress when you turn it on are missed. Synch instruments add overhead on busy servers, so enable them for an investigation and turn them off afterwards.
notes: Some wait classes are not instrumented (mutexes 0 of 173 on, read/write locks 0 of 33 on, shared/exclusive locks 0 of 1 on, condition waits 0 of 79 on, socket i/o 0 of 3 on), so their waits are not in this report. No mutex or rwlock waits here never means no contention.
MariaDB turns the metadata lock instrument (wait/lock/metadata/sql/mdl) off by default; MySQL turns it on.

Wait time is summed across all threads, background threads included, so it can exceed the wall-clock window. Table I/O includes the file I/O and internal lock waits inside each call, which are counted again under their own events, so the classes are never added up.
InnoDB asynchronous I/O (read-ahead, page cleaner writes) is timed only for submitting the request, so its latency is understated. Bytes are exact (see I/O).
Since server start covers 13 min 55 s of uptime; the longest single wait (max) is since start too, never per window.
